quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Negative Adverbs at the Start of a Sentence
quests.faultySentence: Rarely the committee approves a proposal without at least two rounds of revision.
quests.correctedSentence: Rarely does the committee approve a proposal without at least two rounds of revision.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a fronted negative adverb such as 'rarely', the auxiliary comes before the subject and the main verb returns to its base form: 'does the committee approve'.
quests.nativeTip: When a negative adverb like 'rarely' opens the sentence, what happens to the order of the auxiliary and the subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Auxiliary Carries the Tense
quests.faultySentence: Seldom did the manager had to remind the team about deadlines.
quests.incorrectPart: did the manager had to remind
quests.correctedSentence: Seldom did the manager have to remind the team about deadlines.
quests.correctedPart: did the manager have to remind
quests.ruleExplanation: After 'did', the main verb must return to its base form because 'did' already marks the past tense: 'did the manager have to remind'.
quests.nativeTip: Once 'did' carries the past tense in an inverted sentence, what form should the main verb take?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Negative Phrases in Formal Rules
quests.faultySentence: Under no circumstances employees are permitted to share their login credentials.
quests.incorrectPart: Under no circumstances employees are permitted
quests.correctedSentence: Under no circumstances are employees permitted to share their login credentials.
quests.correctedPart: Under no circumstances are employees permitted
quests.ruleExplanation: A fronted negative phrase forces inversion, so the verb 'are' moves before the subject: 'Under no circumstances are employees permitted'.
quests.nativeTip: A negative phrase like 'under no circumstances' opens this rule. Which comes first afterward, the verb or the subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Not Only at the Start of a Sentence
quests.faultySentence: Not only the software crashed, but it also deleted the entire project.
quests.correctedSentence: Not only did the software crash, but it also deleted the entire project.
quests.correctedPart: Not only did the software crash
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Not only' at the start of a sentence triggers inversion with an auxiliary, so the sentence needs 'Not only did the software crash'.
quests.nativeTip: When 'not only' begins a sentence, what must come before the subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: No Sooner ... Than
quests.faultySentence: No sooner had the meeting started when the fire alarm went off.
quests.correctedSentence: No sooner had the meeting started than the fire alarm went off.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', while 'hardly' pairs with 'when', so the sentence needs 'No sooner had the meeting started than'.
quests.nativeTip: 'No sooner' has a fixed partner word, and it is not the one used with 'hardly'. Which word completes the pair?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Hardly ... When
quests.faultySentence: Hardly the guests had arrived when the power went out.
quests.correctedSentence: Hardly had the guests arrived when the power went out.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a fronted 'hardly', the auxiliary moves before the subject, giving 'Hardly had the guests arrived when...'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Hardly' at the start of a sentence works like other negative openers. Which comes first, the subject or 'had'?

quests.conceptTitle: Conditional Inversion: Should + Subject + Base Verb
quests.faultySentence: Should you will need further assistance, please contact our support team.
quests.correctedSentence: Should you need further assistance, please contact our support team.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should you need' replaces 'If you need', and the verb after the subject stays in the base form with no 'will'.
quests.nativeTip: In a formal 'should' conditional, what form of the verb follows the subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Conditional Inversion: Were + Subject + To + Base Verb
quests.faultySentence: Were the company relocate, most employees would lose their jobs.
quests.correctedSentence: Were the company to relocate, most employees would lose their jobs.
quests.ruleExplanation: The inverted form is 'Were' + subject + 'to' + base verb, so 'Were the company to relocate' means 'If the company relocated'.
quests.nativeTip: In an inverted 'were' conditional about a hypothetical future event, which small word links the subject to the verb?

quests.conceptTitle: Conditional Inversion: Had + Subject + Past Participle
quests.faultySentence: Had disclosed the applicant her previous role, the panel would not have questioned her credentials.
quests.correctedSentence: Had the applicant disclosed her previous role, the panel would not have questioned her credentials.
quests.ruleExplanation: Inverted past conditionals put the subject directly after 'had', followed by the past participle: 'Had the applicant disclosed'.
quests.nativeTip: In an inverted past conditional, where does the subject go relative to 'had'?

quests.conceptTitle: Mixed Conditionals: Unreal Past, Present Result
quests.faultySentence: If she accepted the promotion last year, she would be managing the Berlin office now.
quests.incorrectPart: If she accepted the promotion last year
quests.correctedSentence: If she had accepted the promotion last year, she would be managing the Berlin office now.
quests.correctedPart: If she had accepted the promotion last year
quests.ruleExplanation: A mixed conditional linking an unreal past to a present result uses the past perfect in the if-clause: 'had accepted'.
quests.nativeTip: The if-clause refers to a specific past decision that did not happen, while the result is about now. Which tense marks the unreal past?

quests.conceptTitle: Mixed Conditionals: Unreal Present, Past Result
quests.faultySentence: If I am more organized, I would have finished the report before the deadline last week.
quests.correctedSentence: If I were more organized, I would have finished the report before the deadline last week.
quests.ruleExplanation: An unreal present condition uses the past subjunctive 'were', so 'If I were more organized' pairs with the past result 'would have finished'.
quests.nativeTip: The if-clause describes a general quality that isn't true, while the result happened in the past. Which form marks the unreal present?

quests.conceptTitle: Mixed Conditionals: Would + Base Verb for Present Result
quests.faultySentence: If the firm had not lost its main client, it would still employed two hundred people today.
quests.correctedSentence: If the firm had not lost its main client, it would still employ two hundred people today.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the result concerns today, the main clause uses 'would' plus the base verb: 'would still employ'.
quests.nativeTip: The result is about the present day, so what verb form follows 'would'?

quests.conceptTitle: Cleft Sentences: It + Be + Emphasized Noun + Who/That
quests.faultySentence: It was the manager which announced the changes, not the director.
quests.incorrectPart: It was the manager which announced
quests.correctedSentence: It was the manager who announced the changes, not the director.
quests.correctedPart: It was the manager who announced
quests.ruleExplanation: The emphasized noun is a person acting as the subject, so the cleft sentence uses 'who': 'It was the manager who announced'.
quests.nativeTip: In a cleft sentence that emphasizes a person doing the action, which relative word follows?

quests.conceptTitle: Emphasis Structures: What-Clauses as Subjects
quests.faultySentence: What the client needs it is a clearer timeline, not more features.
quests.incorrectPart: What the client needs it is
quests.correctedSentence: What the client needs is a clearer timeline, not more features.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'What the client needs' already works as the subject of the sentence, so adding 'it' repeats the subject unnecessarily.
quests.nativeTip: Does the 'what' clause need an extra pronoun before the verb 'is'?

quests.conceptTitle: Cleft Sentences: It Was Not Until ... That
quests.faultySentence: It was not until the results were published then the team realized the error.
quests.correctedSentence: It was not until the results were published that the team realized the error.
quests.ruleExplanation: The pattern is 'It was not until X that Y', so 'that' links the time phrase to the main clause.
quests.nativeTip: In an 'It was not until...' structure, which word introduces the main clause?

quests.conceptTitle: Comparison: The More ... The More
quests.faultySentence: The more you practice, more confident you become.
quests.correctedSentence: The more you practice, the more confident you become.
quests.ruleExplanation: The pattern is 'The more..., the more...', so the second part also needs 'the': 'the more confident you become'.
quests.nativeTip: In a double comparative, both parts need the same marker. What is missing from the second part?

quests.conceptTitle: Comparison: Multipliers with As ... As
quests.faultySentence: This year's attendance was twice as higher as last year's.
quests.correctedSentence: This year's attendance was twice as high as last year's.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'As ... as' takes the base form of the adjective, so the sentence needs 'twice as high as', not 'as higher as'.
quests.nativeTip: Multiplier comparisons like 'twice' work inside 'as ... as'. Should the adjective in the middle take an -er ending?

quests.conceptTitle: Comparison: Completing Interrupted Comparisons
quests.faultySentence: Our response times are as fast, if not faster than, those of our competitors.
quests.incorrectPart: as fast, if not faster than, those
quests.correctedSentence: Our response times are as fast as, if not faster than, those of our competitors.
quests.correctedPart: as fast as, if not faster than, those
quests.ruleExplanation: Each comparison needs its own partner word: 'as fast as' and 'faster than'. Leaving out the first 'as' leaves the first comparison incomplete.
quests.nativeTip: The first comparison is left unfinished by the interruption. Which word completes 'as fast'?

quests.conceptTitle: Subjunctive: Base Verb After Demand Verbs
quests.faultySentence: The board insisted that the CEO resigns immediately.
quests.correctedSentence: The board insisted that the CEO resign immediately.
quests.ruleExplanation: Demand verbs take the base-form subjunctive in the that-clause, so the sentence needs 'resign', not 'resigns'.
quests.nativeTip: After verbs like 'insist' that express a demand, what verb form is used in the that-clause?

quests.conceptTitle: Subjunctive: Negative Form After Order Verbs
quests.faultySentence: The judge ordered that the defendant does not contact the witness.
quests.incorrectPart: that the defendant does not contact
quests.correctedSentence: The judge ordered that the defendant not contact the witness.
quests.ruleExplanation: The negative subjunctive places 'not' before the base verb without 'do': 'that the defendant not contact the witness'.
quests.nativeTip: In a subjunctive that-clause, how is a negative formed? Is 'do' or 'does' needed?

quests.conceptTitle: Subjunctive: Base Verb After Require That
quests.faultySentence: The regulations require that all drivers to carry proof of insurance.
quests.correctedSentence: The regulations require that all drivers carry proof of insurance.
quests.ruleExplanation: A that-clause after 'require' takes the base verb directly: 'that all drivers carry', with no 'to'.
quests.nativeTip: After 'require that', does the verb need 'to', an -ing ending, or the plain base form?

quests.conceptTitle: Future Perfect: Completion Before a Future Point
quests.faultySentence: By the time the new director arrives next month, we will complete the entire audit.
quests.correctedSentence: By the time the new director arrives next month, we will have completed the entire audit.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By the time' plus a future point calls for the future perfect, which shows an action already complete: 'we will have completed'.
quests.nativeTip: The audit will already be finished before another future moment. Which tense shows completion by then?

quests.conceptTitle: Tense Sequence: Time Clauses in a Past Frame
quests.faultySentence: She said she would call as soon as she will reach the hotel.
quests.incorrectPart: as soon as she will reach
quests.correctedSentence: She said she would call as soon as she reached the hotel.
quests.ruleExplanation: A time clause does not take 'will', and here the past frame set by 'said' and 'would call' calls for the simple past: 'as soon as she reached'.
quests.nativeTip: The sentence is set in the past after 'said'. Which tense fits the time clause after 'as soon as'?

quests.conceptTitle: Tense Sequence: Past Perfect Continuous with Simple Past
quests.faultySentence: The patient had been recovering well until the infection returns last week.
quests.incorrectPart: until the infection returns last week
quests.correctedSentence: The patient had been recovering well until the infection returned last week.
quests.correctedPart: until the infection returned last week
quests.ruleExplanation: The interrupting event happened at a finished past time, so it takes the simple past: 'returned'. The earlier ongoing recovery stays in the past perfect continuous.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase 'last week' points to a finished past event that interrupted the earlier recovery. Which tense fits?

quests.conceptTitle: Embedded Clauses: Whom After a Preposition
quests.faultySentence: The committee questioned to who the funds had been transferred.
quests.correctedSentence: The committee questioned to whom the funds had been transferred.
quests.ruleExplanation: A pronoun that follows a preposition takes the object form, so 'to whom' is correct, not 'to who'.
quests.nativeTip: After a preposition in formal writing, which pronoun form is used for a person?

quests.conceptTitle: Agreement: Subject with an Embedded That-Clause
quests.faultySentence: The fact that the results were published early raise questions about the review process.
quests.correctedSentence: The fact that the results were published early raises questions about the review process.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The fact that...' is a singular noun phrase, and the plural 'results' sits inside its clause, so the main verb is 'raises'.
quests.nativeTip: What is the true subject of the verb: 'the fact' or 'the results'?

quests.conceptTitle: Embedded Clauses: Statement Word Order in Noun Clauses
quests.faultySentence: The auditor wanted to know how much would the repairs cost.
quests.incorrectPart: how much would the repairs cost
quests.correctedSentence: The auditor wanted to know how much the repairs would cost.
quests.correctedPart: how much the repairs would cost
quests.ruleExplanation: Embedded questions keep statement word order, so the subject comes before the modal: 'how much the repairs would cost'.
quests.nativeTip: An embedded question inside 'wanted to know' uses statement order. Which comes first, the subject or 'would'?

quests.conceptTitle: Inversion: Only + Adverbial at the Start of a Sentence
quests.faultySentence: Only after the results had been verified the board agreed to publish the study.
quests.correctedSentence: Only after the results had been verified did the board agree to publish the study.
quests.correctedPart: did the board agree to publish
quests.ruleExplanation: A fronted 'only' phrase triggers inversion in the main clause, so the sentence needs 'did the board agree' with the base verb.
quests.nativeTip: When 'only after...' opens the sentence, what happens to the word order in the main clause?

quests.conceptTitle: Agreement: One Of Which
quests.faultySentence: The chemicals, one of which are highly toxic, must be stored separately.
quests.correctedSentence: The chemicals, one of which is highly toxic, must be stored separately.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'One' is the subject even though 'which' refers to the plural chemicals, so the verb is singular: 'one of which is'.
quests.nativeTip: In 'one of which', which word is the real subject of the verb?

quests.conceptTitle: Parallelism: Not Only ... But Also
quests.faultySentence: The study found that participants who exercised regularly not only slept better but also reporting less stress than those who did not.
quests.correctedSentence: The study found that participants who exercised regularly not only slept better but also reported less stress than those who did not.
quests.ruleExplanation: Keeping both verbs in the simple past, 'slept' and 'reported', makes the 'not only ... but also' structure parallel.
quests.nativeTip: Both parts of 'not only ... but also' need matching verb forms. What form follows 'slept'?
